Capital Gains Indexation Calculator
Sec 48 / New Sec 72 — Cost Inflation Index (CII) based indexation for LTCG computation.
Grandfathering (Sec 73, 5th Proviso): For land or building acquired before 23-Jul-2024, the taxpayer may choose the lower of: (a) Tax @20% with indexation, or (b) Tax @12.5% without indexation — even if sold after 23-Jul-2024.
Other assets: Indexation removed w.e.f. 23-Jul-2024. Flat 12.5% LTCG applies. No grandfathering for gold, debt MF, unlisted shares etc.
🥇🥈 Gold & Silver Rates (31st March)
FMV for Capital Gains — Standard gold rate (24 carat, per 10g) and silver rate (per kg) as on 31st March. Useful for computing FMV for gifts, inheritance, and capital gains.

💍 Gold / Silver Ornament Value Calculator
Notes (R-6 Valuation Rules):
1. Ornament value reduced from 24ct rate for: purity (24ct→22ct), making charges, melting loss, dealer margin, alloy content.
2. Reduction rates: Plain bangles: ~14.08% | Other ornaments: ~16.58% | Studded/stone-set: ~20%
3. Silverware/utensils were liable for Wealth Tax (abolished w.e.f. AY 2016-17).

ICDS — Income Computation & Disclosure Standards
Notified u/s 145(2) — applicable to all assessees following mercantile system (except individuals/HUFs not subject to tax audit)
No.TitleKey Point
IAccounting PoliciesFundamental accounting assumptions: going concern, consistency, accrual. Marked-to-market loss not recognised.
IIValuation of InventoriesCost or NRV, whichever lower. Standard cost/retail method allowed. FIFO/weighted average. No LIFO.
IIIConstruction ContractsPercentage of completion method mandatory. Contract revenue = consideration + variations + claims + incentives.
IVRevenue RecognitionGoods: when property transfers + no significant uncertainty. Services: proportionate completion.
VTangible Fixed AssetsCost model only (no revaluation). Depreciation as per IT Act. Stand-by costs capitalised.
VIEffects of Changes in Foreign Exchange RatesInitial recognition at transaction date rate. Monetary items at closing rate. Exchange differences in P&L.
VIIGovernment GrantsNot recognised until reasonable assurance of compliance + receipt. Revenue grants to P&L; asset grants reduce cost or deferred income.
VIIISecuritiesRecognition at cost (actual or weighted average). Listed: lower of cost or NRV at category level. Unlisted: at cost.
IXBorrowing CostsQualifying asset: capitalise. Others: expense. Includes interest, amortisation of discounts, ancillary costs.
XProvisions, Contingent Liabilities & AssetsProvision: present obligation + probable outflow + reliable estimate. Contingent liabilities: not recognised. Contingent assets: never recognised.

Interest Calculator — Sec 234A / 234B / 234C
New: Sec 423/424/425 • Late filing, Advance tax default & deferment interest
How it works:
234A (Late Filing): 1% per month (or part) on unpaid tax from due date to actual filing date. Tax = Assessed tax − Advance tax − TDS.
234B (Advance Tax Default): 1% per month from Apr 1 to filing date on shortfall. Applies if advance tax paid < 90% of assessed tax.
234C (Deferment): 1% × 3 months per quarter if installment paid < required %. Jun: 15%, Sep: 45%, Dec: 75%, Mar: 100%.

Practitioner Brief — Key Takeaways
What changes · what stays the same under IT Act 2025
1. No change in residency tests
Sec 6 of IT Act 2025 retains the 182-day, 60+365, and visiting Indian/PIO rules identically. Only section numbering changes.
2. Deemed residency relocated to Sec 6(7)
Earlier Sec 6(1A) — same ₹15 lakh income threshold, same "not liable to tax elsewhere" condition.
3. NOR now in Sec 6(13)
Both continuity tests — 9 out of 10 preceding years and 729 days in 7 preceding years — preserved.
4. Special NRI regime moved to Sec 212–217
Substantive provisions — rates, reinvestment formula (A=B×C/D), 3-year lock-in, claw-back — reproduced without material change.
5. NRE interest exemption kept
Moved from Sec 10(4)(ii) to Schedule IV. Linkage remains to FEMA residential status — not income-tax residency.
6. Sec 72 replaces first proviso to Sec 48
Non-residents continue to compute capital gains on shares/debentures in original foreign currency, then reconvert.
7. Residency for pre-01.04.2026 years stays under 1961 Act
Even if assessment/reassessment is completed later. Sec 536 saves the old Act's application to those tax years.
8. Cross-year stays — test each year separately
Stay in FY 2025-26 is governed by 1961 Act; FY 2026-27 by 2025 Act. But look-back days from earlier years are still counted.
9. Sec 115F claw-back survives repeal
Liability is fixed by the section that granted the original exemption (1961 Act); year of taxability for post-01.04.2026 transfer falls under the 2025 Act.
10. Elections & declarations preserved
Sec 115-I opt-out and Sec 115H continuation declarations remain valid by virtue of Sec 536(2)(f).
Reinvestment Exemption — Sec 215
On LTCG from transfer of a foreign exchange asset
ElementDetail
TriggerTransfer of a long-term foreign exchange asset by a non-resident Indian
Reinvestment windowWithin 6 months of the date of transfer
Specified assets for reinvestmentAnother foreign exchange asset or specified savings certificate (as notified)
Exemption formulaA = B × C / D   where — A = LTCG not chargeable; B = LTCG on transfer; C = cost of new asset; D = net consideration
Lock-inNew asset must not be transferred or converted into money within 3 years from date of acquisition
Claw-backExempted LTCG becomes chargeable in the year of premature transfer / conversion of the new asset
Post 01.04.2026 triggering eventIf original exemption was under Sec 115F (1961 Act) and new asset is transferred within lock-in after 01.04.2026 — claw-back liability arises under Sec 115F(2) of the 1961 Act; year of taxability assessed under 2025 Act
Worked illustration: NRI transfers forex asset for net consideration ₹80 lakh, LTCG ₹30 lakh. Reinvests ₹60 lakh in specified asset within 6 months. → Exempt LTCG = 30 × 60 / 80 = ₹22.5 lakh; balance ₹7.5 lakh taxable under Sec 214 at 10%/12.5% depending on transfer date.
Practice note: All rules and forms under the Income-tax Act, 2025 stand notified. Read Sec 536 of the new Act with the savings clause to resolve any cross-statute residency or NRI-regime issue for FY 2025-26 and earlier years. For visiting Indian citizens earning > ₹15 lakh, the modified 120-day + 365-day test applies — this is distinct from the standard 60+365 test.

Tax Planning Strategies IT Act 1961 & IT Act 2025 • Updated for FY 2025-26

Salary Optimisation — Structuring compensation packages and leveraging expanded perquisite exemptions introduced by Finance Act 2025. Most tips apply to the old regime unless marked otherwise.
💰
Structure a Higher Basic Pay for Compounding Benefits
1961: Sec 10(13A), 172025: Sec 15–19
  • Higher basic salary triggers cascading benefits — employer PF contribution (exempt up to 12% of salary) increases, gratuity ceiling improves, commuted pension benefits grow.
  • HRA exemption also rises proportionally with basic pay.
  • Net effect is often a lower effective tax rate when compounding exemptions are factored in.
  • Evaluate the trade-off with your employer’s HR team using actual numbers.
  • This strategy works only under the old regime where HRA and other allowances are exempt.
Old RegimeSalary Structure
🏥
Expanded Perquisite Exemptions — Finance Act 2025
1961: Sec 17(2)2025: Sec 17Both Regimes
  • Overall perquisite exemption cap under Sec 17(2)(iii): ₹50,000 → ₹4,00,000 (effective FY 2025-26).
  • Children’s education allowance: ₹100 → ₹3,000/month per child.
  • Hostel expenditure allowance: ₹300 → ₹9,000/month per child.
  • Free education in employer’s school: threshold ₹1,000 → ₹3,000/month per child.
  • These perquisite exemptions apply under both old and new regimes — a rare dual benefit.
Both RegimesFY 2025-26NEW
🏗
HRA Metro City List Expanded — 4 New Cities Added
1961: Sec 10(13A)2025: Sec 19
  • HRA exemption: 50% of salary for metro cities vs 40% for non-metros.
  • From FY 2025-26, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune and Ahmedabad join Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata in the metro list.
  • On a ₹10 lakh salary, the metro vs non-metro gap translates to ₹1 lakh additional exempt HRA.
  • HRA exemption is not available under the new regime — applicable only under the old regime.
Old RegimeFY 2025-26NEW
📈
NPS Employer Contribution — Now 14% for All Employees
1961: Sec 80CCD(2)2025: Sec 124Both Regimes
  • Employer NPS contribution deduction raised from 10% to 14% of basic salary for all employees (was 14% only for central government).
  • Available under both old and new tax regimes — one of the few dual-regime deductions.
  • On ₹12 lakh basic salary: ₹1.68 lakh tax-free vs the earlier ₹1.2 lakh.
  • Negotiate this as part of your CTC — most employers are willing to restructure.
Pro tip: Even under the new regime where most 80C deductions are gone, NPS employer contribution remains fully deductible. Negotiate this as part of your CTC.
Both RegimesNPSNEW
📱
Non-Monetary Perquisites That Remain Tax-Free
1961: Sec 17(2), Rule 32025: Sec 17, Rule 15
  • Telephone/mobile reimbursement — fully exempt.
  • Laptops, computers for official use — no perquisite value.
  • Free refreshments during working hours — exempt.
  • Meal vouchers: up to ₹50 per meal via non-transferable vouchers.
  • Gifts from employer: up to ₹5,000/year exempt.
  • Movable assets transferred after 10+ years of employer use — no perquisite.
  • Cash medical allowance is fully taxable, but employer-provided health insurance or hospital treatment is exempt.
  • Always prefer in-kind benefits over cash equivalents.
Both RegimesPerquisites
⏰
Time Your Retirement for Maximum Exemption
1961: Sec 10(10), 10(10A), 10(10AA)2025: Sec 11, 19
  • Gratuity: exempt up to ₹25 lakh for private employees; fully exempt for government employees.
  • Leave encashment on retirement: exempt up to ₹25 lakh.
  • Commuted pension: partially or fully exempt depending on gratuity receipt.
  • Standard deduction: ₹75,000 available under both regimes.
  • Timing retirement at start of a financial year gives an entire year to plan utilisation of remaining income.
RetirementUpdated Limits
Capital Gains Planning — Strategic timing and reinvestment to reduce tax. From 23-Jul-2024: LTCG uniformly taxed at 12.5% without indexation; STCG on listed securities at 20%. “Previous Year” is now “Tax Year” under IT Act 2025.
⏰
Holding Period Matters — 12 or 24 Months
1961: Sec 2(42A)2025: Sec 73
  • Listed shares and equity mutual funds: 12 months for LTCG.
  • All other assets (immovable property, unlisted shares, gold, debt funds, etc.): 24 months for LTCG.
  • The earlier 36-month category has been eliminated.
  • LTCG taxed at flat 12.5%; STCG on listed securities at 20%.
  • Plan transfers to cross the applicable holding threshold — the rate difference is significant.
  • If a previous owner (gift/inheritance) held the asset, their holding period is added to yours.
Note: There is no 36-month holding category anymore. All non-listed assets are now 24 months for LTCG classification.
LTCGHolding PeriodUPDATED
🏠
Reinvest in a House — But Know Whether to Invest CG or Net Consideration
1961: Sec 54, 54F2025: Sec 85, 89
  • Sec 54 (Sec 85): On selling a residential house, invest the capital gains amount in a new house for full exemption.
  • Sec 54F (Sec 89): On selling any other long-term asset, invest the entire net sale consideration for full exemption; partial investment gives only proportionate relief.
  • This is the single most confused area in CG planning — know the difference.
Example: You sell shares for ₹1 crore (cost ₹40 lakh, CG = ₹60 lakh). Under Sec 54F, you must invest the full ₹1 crore in a house for 100% exemption. Investing only ₹60 lakh (the CG) gives you only 60% exemption.
  • Purchase: within 1 year before or 2 years after the sale date.
  • Construction: within 3 years of the sale date.
  • Overall cap: ₹10 crore (from AY 2024-25).
  • Two houses allowed if CG ≤ ₹2 crore (once-in-lifetime option).
Sec 54/54FCritical Difference
🔗
54EC Bonds — The 6-Month Non-Negotiable Window
1961: Sec 54EC2025: Sec 85
  • Invest capital gains from sale of long-term land/building in NHAI/REC/NABARD/PFC/IRFC bonds within 6 months.
  • Maximum investment: ₹50 lakh per FY.
  • Lock-in period: 5 years (3 years for pre-Apr-2018 investments).
  • No CGAS extension available — miss the 6-month window and exemption is permanently lost.
  • Apply for bonds well in advance as allotment can take weeks.
Sec 54ECBondsStrict Deadline
🏦
Capital Gains Account Scheme — Your Safety Net
1961: Sec 54(2), 54F(4)2025: Sec 85–89
  • If you cannot find/purchase the new property before ITR due date, deposit the required amount in a Capital Gains Account Scheme (CGAS).
  • Available with authorised banks — Type-A (savings) or Type-B (term deposit).
  • Preserves your exemption claim under Sec 54/54F.
  • Withdraw funds as needed when you find and purchase the property.
  • If amount is not utilised within the allowed window (2 years purchase / 3 years construction), unused balance is taxed as capital gains in the year the time limit expires.
CGAS not available for Sec 54EC bonds. The 6-month bond deadline is absolute.
CGASExtension
🔒
Respect the Lock-in — Early Sale Triggers Full Clawback
1961: Sec 54–54GA2025: Sec 85–91
  • Lock-in periods: 3 years for property (Sec 54/54F), 5 years for bonds (Sec 54EC).
  • Selling the new asset before lock-in expiry triggers full reversal — exempted gain becomes taxable in the year of premature sale.
  • Transfers by gift, will, inheritance, or dissolution of firm are generally not treated as transfer — no clawback.
  • Taking a loan against 54EC bonds within 5 years also triggers reversal.
Lock-inClawback
📊
Harvest the ₹1.25 Lakh LTCG Exemption Annually
1961: Sec 112A2025: Sec 198
  • LTCG on listed equity/equity MFs exempt up to ₹1.25 lakh per year (raised from ₹1 lakh from FY 2024-25).
  • “Harvest” gains by selling profitable holdings up to ₹1.25 lakh in gains each year and immediately repurchasing.
  • This resets your cost base higher, reducing future taxable gains.
  • With an HUF, you get a second ₹1.25 lakh exemption in the HUF’s name.
Tax HarvestingEquityUPDATED
House Property — Optimising annual value computation, interest deductions, and ownership planning under both regimes.
🏠
Select the Right 2 Properties as Self-Occupied
1961: Sec 23(2)2025: Sec 21
  • Designate up to 2 properties as self-occupied (annual value = Nil).
  • Remaining properties are deemed let-out — notional rent taxed at 30% after standard deduction.
  • Choose your two highest-value properties as self-occupied to minimise deemed income.
  • Self-occupied: interest deduction up to ₹2,00,000.
  • Let-out: unlimited interest deduction allowed.
  • Sometimes keeping a mortgaged property as “let-out” and claiming full interest is more beneficial.
Under the new regime (Sec 202), the ₹2 lakh interest deduction for self-occupied property is NOT available. Only interest for let-out property is allowed.
Self-OccupiedDeemed Let-out
💲
Pre-Construction Interest — The Hidden 5-Year Deduction
1961: Sec 24(b)2025: Sec 22
  • Interest paid during construction (before possession) is deductible in 5 equal annual instalments from the year of completion.
  • This is in addition to the regular Sec 24(b) interest deduction.
  • Construction must complete within 5 years from end of FY of borrowing — otherwise limit drops from ₹2 lakh to just ₹30,000 for self-occupied property.
  • Keep all bank statements and builder receipts as evidence.
Pre-constructionSec 24(b)
🗃
Municipal Tax — Payment Basis, Not Accrual
1961: Sec 23(1)2025: Sec 21
  • Municipal taxes deductible only when actually paid, not when due or accrued.
  • Clear pending property tax arrears in a high-income year to maximise the tax benefit.
  • Conversely, don’t prepay if your income this year is below the taxable threshold.
Municipal TaxPayment Basis
👥
Joint Home Loan for Double the Interest Benefit
1961: Sec 24(b), 80C2025: Sec 22, 123
  • Both earning spouses can co-own the property and take a joint home loan.
  • Each co-owner claims up to ₹2 lakh interest (Sec 24) and ₹1.5 lakh principal (Sec 80C) separately.
  • Household total: ₹4 lakh interest + ₹3 lakh principal — double the individual benefit.
  • Both names must be on the property deed.
  • Both must contribute to EMI payments from their own bank accounts.
  • This benefit is available only under the old regime.
Joint LoanOld Regime
Business & Profession — Deduction management, compliance timing, and regime selection for business taxpayers.
💳
Sec 43B Payments — Pay Before Return Due Date
1961: Sec 43B2025: Sec 37
  • PF/ESI, bonus, leave encashment, interest on institutional loans, and taxes — deductible only on actual payment.
  • Ensure these are paid before the ITR due date.
  • MSME vendor payments must be made within 45 days (or 15 days without written agreement).
  • Delayed MSME payments are disallowed entirely as a business expense, not merely deferred.
Sec 43BMSMEUPDATED
🛒
Digital Payments — Always Above ₹10,000
1961: Sec 40A(3)2025: Sec 36
  • Cash payment exceeding ₹10,000 to one person on one day is entirely disallowed as a business deduction.
  • For transporters, the limit is ₹35,000.
  • Also applies to capital expenditure where depreciation is claimed.
  • Use UPI, NEFT, RTGS, or cheque for all significant payments.
  • Maintain a strict no-cash policy above the threshold to protect every deduction claim.
Cash LimitSec 40A(3)
📚
Presumptive Taxation — Higher Thresholds from FY 2024-25
1961: Sec 44AD, 44ADA2025: Sec 58–62
  • Business turnover up to ₹3 crore (95%+ digital receipts) or ₹2 crore (otherwise) — opt for presumptive taxation at 8%/6%.
  • Professionals: up to ₹75 lakh (95%+ digital) or ₹50 lakh.
  • Income deemed at fixed percentages — no need for full books or tax audit.
  • Ideal for freelancers, consultants, and small traders wanting minimal compliance.
PresumptiveUPDATED
🛠
Depreciation — 180-Day Rule for Full-Year Claim
1961: Sec 322025: Sec 33
  • Assets used for less than 180 days in the first year get only 50% depreciation.
  • Install new plant/machinery before 30 September to claim full-year depreciation.
  • Manufacturing units get additional depreciation of 20% on new (not second-hand) plant and machinery — one-time extra benefit in the year of installation.
Depreciation180-Day Rule
Smart Strategies — Regime selection, family tax planning, and advanced techniques that work across income heads.
⚖️
Old vs New Regime — The ₹3.75 Lakh Break-Even
1961: Sec 115BAC2025: Sec 202
  • New regime (default from AY 2024-25) has lower slab rates but disallows HRA, LTA, 80C, 80D, housing loan interest (for SOP), and most allowances.
  • Basic exemption threshold under new regime: ₹4,00,000.
  • Salaried employees can switch each year; business taxpayers cannot switch back once they opt out.
  • Old regime is better if total deductions/exemptions exceed approximately ₹3.75 lakh.
  • New regime: ₹75,000 standard deduction + tax rebate up to ₹12 lakh income — earners below ₹12.75 lakh effectively pay zero tax.
Note: Business/profession taxpayers who opt out of the new regime cannot switch back. Salaried individuals have annual flexibility. Most allowances and exemptions (HRA, LTA, children education allowance, etc.) are not available under the new regime.

👪
HUF — A Separate Taxpayer for Your Family
1961: Sec 2(31)2025: Sec 2
  • HUF gets its own PAN, its own basic exemption limit (₹4 lakh under new regime), and its own set of deductions.
  • Route income like rent from ancestral property, business profits, and investment returns through the HUF.
  • The ₹1.25 lakh LTCG equity exemption applies separately to the HUF.
  • Gifts from HUF members to the HUF are tax-free.
  • One of the most underutilised tax-planning structures available to Hindu families.

80C Toolkit — ₹1.5 Lakh + ₹50K NPS + ₹1 Lakh Health
1961: Sec 80C, 80CCD, 80D2025: Sec 123–125
  • 80C: ₹1,50,000 (EPF, PPF, ELSS, NSC, tuition, home loan principal).
  • 80CCD(1B): ₹50,000 (NPS self-contribution).
  • 80D: up to ₹1,00,000 (health insurance for self + senior citizen parents).
  • Total possible deductions: ₹3 lakh.
  • ELSS has the shortest lock-in (3 years) among 80C instruments with equity returns.
  • PPF is risk-free at 7.1% with 15-year lock-in.
  • These deductions are available only under the old regime.

Avoid Clubbing — Gift Wisely to Family Members
1961: Sec 642025: Sec 99
  • Income from assets transferred to spouse or minor child without adequate consideration is clubbed with the transferor.
  • Gift to adult children (18+) — no clubbing at all.
  • Gift to parents — income taxed in their hands at likely lower rates.
  • Property transferred to minor — sell only after the child turns 18 to avoid clubbing of capital gains.
  • Income earned by spouse from their own skill or effort (salary, professional fees) is never clubbed even if initial capital was gifted.

Startup Tax Holiday — Extended to 2030
1961: Sec 80IAC2025: Sec 131
  • DPIIT-recognised startups incorporated up to 1 April 2030 (extended from 2025) can claim 100% tax holiday for 3 consecutive years out of the first 10 years.
  • Turnover must not exceed ₹100 crore in any of the claim years.
  • Angel tax (Sec 56(2)(viib)) has been abolished entirely from FY 2024-25 for all investor classes.
  • Significant boost for founders raising early-stage funding.
